key_terms.meaning: The system is the quantity of matter or region chosen for study; the boundary (control surface) is the real or imaginary surface that separates it from the surroundings
A system of fixed mass; no mass crosses the boundary, though heat and work may
A region of fixed location through which mass may flow in and out
A system that exchanges neither mass nor energy (heat or work) with the surroundings
A system whose properties are the same at every point, e.g. a single gas phase
A system with more than one phase or region, so properties jump at interfaces
A property independent of the size of the system, e.g. T, P, density ρ, molar volume v
A property proportional to the amount of matter, e.g. mass m, volume V, total internal energy U; dividing by mass gives a specific property
An extensive property divided by the number of moles n, e.g. molar volume v = V/n in m³/mol
A property fixed once the state is fixed; its change depends only on the end states, e.g. U, H, T, P
A quantity whose value depends on the route between the end states, e.g. work W and heat Q
An ideal process that proceeds through a continuous series of equilibrium states and can be reversed exactly by an infinitesimal change in the surroundings
Any real process with friction, finite gradients or unrestrained expansion, so it cannot be reversed without extra work input from outside
Energy in transition across the boundary due to a driving force and a displacement; for a simple compressible system δW = P dV
Energy in transition across the boundary because of a temperature difference; δQ is not an exact differential
If A is in thermal equilibrium with C and B is in thermal equilibrium with C, then A and B are in equilibrium with each other; this makes temperature a property
An adiabatic wall blocks heat transfer; a diathermal wall allows heat transfer so that equilibrium can be reached

key_terms.term: First law for a closed system
key_terms.meaning: ΔU = Q − W for a change of state, and ∮δQ = ∮δW for a cycle; U is a state function
For an open system at steady state with one inlet and one outlet: Q − W<sub>s</sub> = ṁ[Δh + Δ(c²/2) + gΔz], with c the stream speed
Flow work Pv is the work done to push fluid in and out; adding it to internal energy gives enthalpy H = U + PV
C<sub>v</sub> = (∂U/∂T)<sub>v</sub> and C<sub>p</sub> = (∂H/∂T)<sub>p</sub>, in J/(mol·K) or kJ/(kg·K)
Ducts that convert enthalpy into kinetic energy (nozzle, pressure falls) or kinetic energy into enthalpy (diffuser, pressure rises); both are nearly adiabatic with no shaft work
Unsteady open system: u<sub>2</sub> = h<sub>line</sub>; for an ideal gas T<sub>2</sub> = γT<sub>line</sub>
w<sub>in</sub> = ∫v dP; isothermal RT ln(P<sub>2</sub>/P<sub>1</sub>), isentropic c<sub>p</sub>T<sub>1</sub>[(P<sub>2</sub>/P<sub>1</sub>)<sup>(γ−1)/γ</sup> − 1]
Compressor η<sub>c</sub> = w<sub>isentropic</sub>/w<sub>actual</sub>; turbine η<sub>t</sub> = w<sub>actual</sub>/w<sub>isentropic</sub>
P*/P<sub>0</sub> = [2/(γ + 1)]<sup>γ/(γ−1)</sup>: 0.528 for air, about 0.546 for superheated steam; below it the nozzle is choked

takeaways: A thermodynamic system is defined only after you draw the boundary; every balance is written for what crosses that boundary.
Intensive properties locate the state; extensive properties scale with amount and become specific or molar properties after dividing by mass or moles.
State functions depend only on where you start and end; work and heat depend on the road taken between them.
Energy is stored as internal, kinetic or potential energy, or is in transit as heat or work; only transit terms cross the boundary.
The zeroth law is what makes temperature measurable, and the ideal-gas scale lets any gas thermometer agree with the rest.
ΔU = Q − W for a closed system is the whole first law; Joule's paddle-wheel experiment is what tells us U is a state function.
Enthalpy is not a new kind of energy, only U + PV, and it enters open-system balances because the fluid carries flow work in and out.
C<sub>v</sub> and C<sub>p</sub> convert temperature changes into internal-energy and enthalpy changes; for an ideal gas C<sub>p</sub> − C<sub>v</sub> = R.
In a nozzle enthalpy turns into kinetic energy and in a throttling valve enthalpy stays constant; a compressor needs w<sub>in</sub> = ∫v dP, least when isothermal.
A gas speeds up in a narrowing duct only below Mach 1; supersonic flow needs a diverging section, and below the critical pressure ratio a nozzle is choked.
bank_note: Long answers combine a clean statement of the law with a labelled control volume, a correctly signed energy balance and a numerical substitution in consistent units. Most syllabi ask for the first law for flow and non-flow processes, Joule's experiment and the steady-flow energy equation with a nozzle, turbine or compressor; definitions and classifications carry easy marks, so start with them.

bank.q: Define a thermodynamic system and its boundary. Distinguish closed, open and isolated systems and give one plant example of each. Classify these as intensive or extensive: pressure, volume, molar volume, density, temperature, total enthalpy, mass, specific heat capacity.
outline: System = whatever lies inside the chosen boundary; boundary is real or imaginary
Closed: fixed mass, energy may cross (piston-cylinder gas)
Open: mass crosses (pump, heat exchanger, turbine)
Isolated: neither mass nor energy crosses (perfectly insulated rigid vessel)
Intensive: pressure, temperature, density, molar volume, specific heat capacity
Extensive: volume, mass, total enthalpy
Dividing an extensive property by mass or moles gives a specific or molar (intensive) property
answer: Define the terms. A system is the quantity of matter or the region of space chosen for study. Everything outside it is the surroundings, and the real or imaginary surface between them is the boundary. The boundary may be fixed (a tank wall) or moving (a piston face), and it must be drawn before any balance is written, because every energy balance counts only what crosses it.

Classify by what crosses the boundary. A closed system (control mass) has a fixed mass: no matter crosses, but heat and work may. Plant example: the gas trapped in a reciprocating compressor cylinder while both valves are shut, or a sealed batch autoclave being heated.
An open system (control volume) has mass crossing its boundary. Plant examples: a centrifugal pump, a steam turbine, a shell-and-tube heat exchanger, a length of pipeline.

An isolated system exchanges neither mass nor energy. It is an ideal limit; the nearest plant example is a well-insulated, sealed, rigid storage vessel over a short time, or the system plus its surroundings taken together.

answer.text: Classify the listed properties by the halving test: cut the system into two equal halves and see which values halve.

answer: State the ratio rule. Dividing one extensive property by another gives an intensive one, because the size cancels: density = m/V, specific volume v = V/m, molar volume = V/n, specific enthalpy h = H/m. This is why steam tables can list v, u and h without knowing the size of the plant.

Check with numbers. A vessel of 2.00 kg gas in 1.20 m³ has ρ = 2.00/1.20 = 1.67 kg/m³. Each half holds 1.00 kg in 0.600 m³, so ρ = 1.00/0.600 = 1.67 kg/m³ again: mass and volume halved, density did not. Intensive properties are never added: two tanks at 300 K joined together are still at 300 K, not 600 K.

bank.q: State the zeroth law of thermodynamics and show how it leads to temperature as a property. Describe the constant-volume gas thermometer and explain why the ideal-gas temperature scale does not depend on which gas is used.
outline: Statement of transitivity of thermal equilibrium
Diathermal wall lets systems reach equilibrium; adiabatic wall prevents it
Equilibrium means no observable change and a common value of the property called temperature
Constant-volume gas thermometer: P vs T at fixed V, T = 273.16 × (P/P<sub>tp</sub>) K
All gases give the same limiting value as P → 0, which defines the ideal-gas scale
Relation to Celsius and Kelvin offsets; fixed points (ice point, steam point, triple point)
answer: State the law. If body A is in thermal equilibrium with body B, and B is in thermal equilibrium with body C, then A is in thermal equilibrium with C. Thermal equilibrium means that when the bodies are joined through a diathermal wall (one that lets heat pass), no net heat flows and nothing observable changes. An adiabatic wall blocks heat, so bodies separated by it need not come to equilibrium.

Show that temperature is a property. Because equilibrium is transitive, all bodies in equilibrium with one another share some quantity that has the same value in each of them. That quantity is called temperature. It depends only on the state of each body, so it is a property (and an intensive one). The law also justifies a thermometer: body B is the thermometer; if it gives the same reading when touched to A and to C, then A and C are at the same temperature without ever being brought together.

Build an empirical scale. Pick a thermometric property X that changes with hotness (mercury length, platinum resistance, gas pressure) and set θ = aX + b with two fixed points. For a platinum thermometer reading 100.0 Ω at 0 °C and 138.5 Ω at 100 °C, a reading of 119.4 Ω gives θ = 100 × (119.4 − 100.0)/(138.5 − 100.0) = 50.39 °C. A mercury thermometer at the same body may read slightly differently, because each property is linear in its own way between the fixed points.

answer.text: Describe the constant-volume gas thermometer. A bulb holds a fixed volume of gas, connected to a mercury manometer whose movable limb is raised or lowered to bring the mercury back to a fixed mark, so the gas volume stays constant. The gas pressure P is read from the mercury height. The bulb is first placed at the triple point of water (273.16 K), giving P<sub>tp</sub>; at the unknown temperature the pressure is P.

answer: Explain why the gas does not matter. With a well-filled bulb, hydrogen, nitrogen and helium give slightly different values of T, because real gases are not exactly ideal. Repeat the measurement with less gas in the bulb, so that P<sub>tp</sub> becomes smaller, and extrapolate the readings to P<sub>tp</sub> → 0. In that limit every gas behaves as an ideal gas (PV = nRT, so P ∝ T at constant V), and all gases give the same limiting value. That limit defines the ideal-gas temperature scale: T = 273.16 K × lim (P/P<sub>tp</sub>). It is independent of the gas and coincides with the thermodynamic kelvin scale defined later from the Carnot engine.

Relate the scales. T(K) = t(°C) + 273.15, so the ice point is 273.15 K and the steam point 373.15 K; t(°F) = 1.8 t(°C) + 32; T(R) = t(°F) + 459.67 = 1.8 T(K). Fixed points: ice point 0 °C, steam point 100 °C (both at 1 atm), triple point of water 0.01 °C = 273.16 K. Check: 27 °C = 300.15 K = 80.6 °F = 540.27 R, and 1.8 × 300.15 = 540.27.

bank.q: Distinguish point functions from path functions with examples. Explain what an exact differential is and use it to show that work and heat are not properties of a system.
outline: Point function: fixed by state, change independent of path, has an exact differential
Path function: depends on route, written δW and δQ, no exact differential
Example: 1 kg gas from state 1 to state 2 by different routes gives different W and Q
∮dU = 0 for a cycle, but ∮δQ = ∮δW ≠ 0
Consequence: U, H, T, P can be tabulated; W and Q cannot
answer: Define both kinds. A point (state) function has one value for each state; its change between two states depends only on the end states. Examples: P, V, T, U, H. A path function has a value only for a process, and that value depends on the route taken. Examples: work W and heat Q. Small amounts are written dU for a state function but δW and δQ for path functions, and the total is W, not ΔW.

answer.text: Give the exact-differential test. A differential dX = M(x, y) dx + N(x, y) dy is exact (the change of some function X) when the cross derivatives are equal; then ∮dX = 0 around any cycle.
answer.pre: exact  ⇔  (∂M/∂y) at fixed x  =  (∂N/∂x) at fixed y

answer.text: Apply it to an ideal gas with T and V as the variables (one mole).

head: Differential
M (coefficient of dT)
N (coefficient of dV)
∂M/∂V
∂N/∂T
Exact?
rows: no: W is not a property

answer: Show it with numbers. A gas goes from A (3 kPa, 1 L) to B (1 kPa, 3 L) by two quasi-static paths of straight segments. Path A through (2 L, 1.5 kPa): W = ½(3 + 1.5)(1) + ½(1.5 + 1)(1) = 2.25 + 1.25 = 3.50 J. Path B through (2 L, 2 kPa): W = 2.50 + 1.50 = 4.00 J. Same end states, different work, so W cannot be the change of any property.

Heat follows. For an ideal gas PV = 3 kPa·L at both A and B, so T and U are the same at both ends: ΔU = 0. The first law Q = ΔU + W then gives Q<sub>A</sub> = 3.50 J and Q<sub>B</sub> = 4.00 J: heat also depends on the path, so it is not a property either.

Close with the cycle. Go A → B by path A and back by path B reversed: ∮dU = 0 (U returns to its value), but ∮δW = 3.50 − 4.00 = −0.50 J and ∮δQ = −0.50 J, both non-zero. Consequence: U, H, T and P can be tabulated against state (steam tables), while W and Q can never be tabulated; they must be computed for each process.

bank.q: State the first law of thermodynamics for a closed system undergoing a cycle and for a closed system undergoing a change of state. Describe Joule's paddle-wheel experiment and explain what it proves about internal energy.
outline: Cycle: ∮δQ = ∮δW, so net heat equals net work
Change of state: ΔU = Q − W with sign convention
Joule's experiment: falling weights drive a paddle, insulated vessel of water, measured work and temperature rise
Same temperature rise is produced by a different amount of work or by heating — the mechanical equivalent of heat
Conclusion: U is a state function; the energy change depends only on end states, not on whether work or heat caused it
Limitations of Joule's original measurement and why a state function is needed

answer.text: State the law for a cycle. When a closed system goes through a cycle and returns to its starting state, the net heat taken in equals the net work done:
State it for a change of state. For a closed system going from state 1 to state 2, with Q the heat added and W the work done by the system:
answer.pre:
Q − W = ΔU = U₂ − U₁
with bulk motion and height:  Q − W = ΔU + ΔKE + ΔPE

answer: Explain the link. Apply the cycle law to two cycles that share one return path: going 1 → 2 by path A or by path B and returning by C. Then Q<sub>A</sub> − W<sub>A</sub> = Q<sub>B</sub> − W<sub>B</sub>, so Q − W is the same for every path between 1 and 2. A quantity whose change does not depend on the path is a property: it is called internal energy U.

answer.text: Show the cyclic law on a three-process cycle (the second worked example of the closed-system chapter).

answer: Describe Joule's paddle-wheel experiment. A known mass hangs on a cord wound round a drum; as it falls through height h it turns a paddle wheel inside an insulated vessel of water. The insulation makes Q = 0. The falling mass gives up potential energy mgh as stirring work on the water, so W = −mgh in the ΔU = Q − W convention. Joule measured the temperature rise of the water and repeated the test with different masses and heights.

answer.text: Work a number: 10.0 kg falling 2.00 m stirs 1.00 kg of water (c = 4.18 kJ/(kg·K)).

answer: What the experiment proves. The same rise in water temperature was produced by a fixed amount of work whatever the mass, height or stirring rate, and the same rise can be produced by heating the water with no work at all. So the change of state, and the energy stored, depend only on the end states, not on whether work or heat produced them: internal energy is a state function, and work and heat are two forms of the same energy in transit (about 4.18 kJ raises 1 kg of water by 1 K).

Limitations. The temperature rises are tiny (0.0469 K above), so Joule needed very sensitive thermometers and corrections for heat leaks and the heat capacity of the vessel; modern measurements use electrical work, which is easier to measure precisely. The first law tells how much energy changes, not which processes can happen; that needs the second law.

bank.q: Define internal energy and enthalpy. Derive the constant-volume and constant-pressure heat capacities from the first law and relate C<sub>p</sub>, C<sub>v</sub> and R for an ideal gas.
outline: U is the energy stored at molecular level; absolute value unknown, changes are computed
H = U + PV, a state function, useful for constant-pressure processes
At constant volume, W = 0, so δQ = dU and C<sub>v</sub> = (∂U/∂T)<sub>v</sub>
At constant pressure, δQ = dH and C<sub>p</sub> = (∂H/∂T)<sub>p</sub>
For an ideal gas, U and H depend on T only, so dU = C<sub>v</sub>dT and dH = C<sub>p</sub>dT
C<sub>p</sub> − C<sub>v</sub> = R per mole; γ = C<sub>p</sub>/C<sub>v</sub>
answer: Define internal energy. U is the energy stored in the molecules of the system: their translation, rotation and vibration, and the potential energy of the forces between them, with the system at rest as a whole. Its absolute value is not known; tables fix U = 0 at a reference state and give changes, which is all the first law needs. U is extensive and a state function.
Define enthalpy. H = U + PV. Since U, P and V are properties, H is a property too. It is useful because at constant pressure, and in every flow device, U and the work PV always appear together.

answer.text: Constant volume. For a closed system with only P–V work, δW = P dV = 0 when V is fixed, so the first law gives δQ = dU. The heat per kelvin per mole is then the slope of U:
Constant pressure. Now δW = P dV, so δQ = dU + P dV. At constant P, d(PV) = P dV, so δQ = d(U + PV) = dH:

Ideal gas. Joule's free-expansion result gives U = U(T) only. Then H = U + PV = U + RT per mole is also a function of T only, so dU = C<sub>v</sub> dT and dH = C<sub>p</sub> dT for any process, not only at constant V or P. Differentiate H = U + RT:
answer.pre:
dH/dT = dU/dT + R    ⇒    C<sub>p</sub> = C<sub>v</sub> + R,   γ = C<sub>p</sub>/C<sub>v</sub>
per kg:  c<sub>p</sub> − c<sub>v</sub> = R/M

answer.text: Check with numbers: 2.0 mol, C<sub>v</sub> = 20.8 J/(mol·K), heated 300 → 400 K.

answer: Read the result. ΔU is the same on both paths because U of an ideal gas depends on T only; the extra 1662.8 J at constant pressure is exactly the expansion work nRΔT = 2.0 × 8.314 × 100, which is why C<sub>p</sub> exceeds C<sub>v</sub> by R. For air, C<sub>p</sub>/C<sub>v</sub> = 29.10/20.79 = 1.40.

bank.q: A rigid, insulated vessel holds 2 kg of a gas at 300 K. A paddle wheel does 60 kJ of work on the gas while an electric heater inside the vessel supplies 25 kJ. Find ΔU and the final temperature if c<sub>v</sub> = 0.75 kJ/(kg·K).
outline: Rigid vessel: no boundary work; insulated: no heat from outside
Paddle work and electrical work both cross the boundary as work done on the gas
ΔU = m c<sub>v</sub> ΔT → ΔT = 85/(2 × 0.75) = 56.7 K
Final temperature 356.7 K
If the boundary is drawn so that the heater element is outside the gas, the 25 kJ enters as heat instead; ΔU is the same
answer: Choose the system and convention. System: the gas in the vessel, including the heater element inside the boundary. Q is heat added to the system, W is work done by the system, ΔU = Q − W. The vessel is rigid (no boundary work) and does not move, so ΔKE = ΔPE = 0.

Identify every energy transfer. The vessel is insulated, so no heat crosses from outside: Q = 0. The paddle shaft crosses the boundary and does 60 kJ of work on the gas: W<sub>paddle</sub> = −60 kJ. The heater wires cross the boundary and carry electrical work, 25 kJ done on the system: W<sub>elec</sub> = −25 kJ. Total W = −85 kJ.

answer.text: Apply the first law.
Find the temperature rise from ΔU = m c<sub>v</sub> ΔT (rigid vessel, so c<sub>v</sub> is the right capacity).

answer: Check the other boundary choice. If the boundary is drawn round the gas only, with the hot heater element outside it, the 25 kJ crosses as heat: Q = +25 kJ and W = −60 kJ. Then ΔU = 25 − (−60) = +85 kJ, the same answer. The words "heat" and "work" depend on where the boundary is drawn; ΔU does not.

The common slip. Writing the heater energy as heat (+25) but the paddle work as +60 gives ΔU = 25 − 60 = −35 kJ and a temperature fall of 23.3 K in an insulated vessel that is being stirred and heated, which is impossible. Work done on the system is negative in ΔU = Q − W; write the sign with every term.
Answer. ΔU = +85 kJ and the gas ends at 356.7 K. Both inputs raise U; neither is lost, because the vessel is insulated and rigid.

bank.q: Steam at 1 MPa and 300 °C (h = 3051 kJ/kg, v = 0.2580 m³/kg) enters an insulated nozzle at 40 m/s and leaves at 0.2 MPa and 150 °C (h = 2769 kJ/kg, v = 0.9599 m³/kg). Find the exit velocity, and the inlet and exit areas for 1.5 kg/s. What kind of nozzle is needed?
outline: Steady-flow energy equation with q = 0 and w<sub>s</sub> = 0, height change negligible
h₁ + c₁²/2 = h₂ + c₂²/2; convert kJ/kg to J/kg before adding the kinetic terms
c₂ ≈ 752 m/s
Areas from A = ṁv/c: inlet 96.7 cm², exit 19.1 cm²
Pressure ratio 0.2 is below the critical ratio of about 0.546 for steam, so the flow passes sonic speed: a converging–diverging nozzle
answer: Control volume and assumptions. The nozzle at steady flow, one inlet and one outlet. Insulated: q = 0. No shaft: w<sub>s</sub> = 0. Height change negligible. The energy equation reduces to h₁ + c₁²/2 = h₂ + c₂²/2.

answer.text: Solve for the exit speed in consistent units (J/kg = m²/s²).

answer: Note the size of the inlet kinetic energy: c₁²/2 = 800 J/kg = 0.8 kJ/kg, under 0.3 % of the enthalpy drop. Dropping it gives c₂ = √564 000 = 751.0 m/s, almost the same; in a nozzle the exit kinetic energy is what matters.

answer.text: Areas from the mass balance ṁ = ρAc = Ac/v, so A = ṁv/c.

answer: Decide the shape. The pressure ratio is 0.2/1.0 = 0.2, well below the critical ratio for superheated steam, about 0.546. So the steam reaches sonic speed at a throat and must expand further in a diverging part: the nozzle is converging–diverging. Check with the speed of sound at the exit, a = √(γRT) with γ ≈ 1.3, R = 461.5 J/(kg·K), T = 423 K: a = √(1.3 × 461.5 × 423.15) = 504 m/s, so the exit Mach number is 752/504 = 1.49, supersonic. A purely converging nozzle could not deliver 752 m/s.

What a converging nozzle would do. Its exit could fall only to the critical pressure, about 0.546 × 1 MPa = 0.546 MPa, where the steam reaches sonic speed; the remaining drop to 0.2 MPa would happen outside the nozzle in shock waves and eddies, and the enthalpy it could have converted would be lost.

Why nozzles are nearly adiabatic. The steam spends a few milliseconds in the nozzle, and the wall area is small compared with the energy carried, so heat loss is a tiny fraction of the 282 kJ/kg converted. Answer: c₂ = 752 m/s; inlet area 96.7 cm², exit area 19.1 cm²; a converging–diverging nozzle.

bank.q: A compressor takes air at 100 kPa and 300 K at 90 m/s and delivers it at 500 kPa and 460 K at 20 m/s. The mass flow rate is 0.05 kg/s and heat loss is 3 kW. Find the shaft power required, taking C<sub>p</sub> = 1.005 kJ/(kg·K).
outline: Steady-flow equation: Q − W<sub>s</sub> = ṁ[(h<sub>2</sub> − h<sub>1</sub>) + (c<sub>2</sub>² − c<sub>1</sub>²)/2 + gΔz]
Δh = C<sub>p</sub>ΔT = 1.005 × 160 = 160.8 kJ/kg
Kinetic term (400 − 8100)/2 = −3850 J/kg = −3.85 kJ/kg
Per kg: Q/m = −3/0.05 = −60 kJ/kg
Power = 0.05 × 216.95 ≈ 10.8 kW input; negative sign means work on the system
answer: Control volume, convention and data. The compressor at steady state; Q is heat into the air and W<sub>s</sub> shaft work done by the air. ṁ = 0.05 kg/s; T₁ = 300 K, c₁ = 90 m/s; T₂ = 460 K, c₂ = 20 m/s; heat loss 3 kW, so Q = −3 kW; c<sub>p</sub> = 1.005 kJ/(kg·K); height change neglected. Air is treated as an ideal gas, so Δh = c<sub>p</sub>ΔT.

answer.text: Write the per-kilogram equation and evaluate each term.
Solve for the shaft work.
Power.

answer: Interpret the sign. W<sub>s</sub> is negative, so 10.85 kW of work is done on the air: the motor must supply about 10.8 kW. Of each kilojoule-per-kilogram put in, 160.8 raises the enthalpy, 60 leaves as heat through the casing, and 3.85 is returned because the air leaves slower than it enters.

Effect of dropping the kinetic terms. Without them, −60 − w<sub>s</sub> = 160.8, so w<sub>s</sub> = −220.8 kJ/kg and the power 11.04 kW, 1.8 % too high. Here the air enters fast (90 m/s), so the kinetic term is worth keeping.

answer.text: Check the balance.

bank.q: One mole of an ideal gas at 300 K and 1 bar is heated to 500 K, first at constant volume and then at constant pressure. With C<sub>v</sub> = 20.8 J/(mol·K) and R = 8.314 J/(mol·K), compute Q, W and ΔU for both paths and compare.
outline: Constant volume: W = 0, Q = ΔU = C<sub>v</sub>ΔT = 4160 J
Constant pressure: C<sub>p</sub> = C<sub>v</sub> + R = 29.114; Q = ΔH = 5822.8 J
ΔU = 4160 J on both paths because U of an ideal gas depends on T only (the two end states differ in P and V but share T)
W = Q − ΔU = 1662.8 J = RΔT
The difference in Q equals the expansion work
Sketch both paths on a P–V diagram
answer: Data and convention. n = 1 mol, T₁ = 300 K, P₁ = 1 bar, T₂ = 500 K, C<sub>v</sub> = 20.8 J/(mol·K), R = 8.314 J/(mol·K); C<sub>p</sub> = C<sub>v</sub> + R = 29.114 J/(mol·K). ΔU = Q − W with W done by the gas. ΔT = 200 K.

answer.text: Locate the states. V₁ = RT₁/P₁ = 8.314 × 300/10⁵ = 0.02494 m³.
Constant-volume path 1 → 2v.
answer.pre:
W = ∫P dV = 0
ΔU = n C<sub>v</sub> ΔT = 1 × 20.8 × 200 = 4160 J
Q = ΔU + W = 4160 J

answer.text: Constant-pressure path 1 → 2p.

Sketch on a P–V diagram: the constant-volume path is a vertical line at V = 0.02494 m³ from 1 to 1.667 bar, with no area under it; the constant-pressure path is a horizontal line at 1 bar from 0.02494 to 0.04157 m³, with area 1662.8 J under it.

svg.aria: P-V sketch with a vertical constant-volume path and a horizontal constant-pressure path from the same start

answer: Compare. ΔU = 4160 J on both paths. The end states are not the same (2v is at 1.667 bar, 2p at 1 bar), but they share T = 500 K, and the internal energy of an ideal gas depends on T only. Q differs by 5822.8 − 4160 = 1662.8 J, exactly the expansion work done at constant pressure: work and heat depend on the path, ΔU does not.

bank.q: A gas in a piston-cylinder assembly expands from 2 bar and 0.1 m³ to 0.3 m³. Compute the work done when the expansion is (a) isobaric, (b) reversible isothermal (ideal gas), (c) into a vacuum. Which gives the most work, and why does that not contradict the rule that a reversible process gives the most work between the same two end states?
outline: Sign convention: work done by the system is positive, W = ∫P dV for a slow process
Isobaric: W = P(V₂ − V₁) = 200 × 0.2 = 40 kJ
Isothermal: W = P₁V₁ ln(V₂/V₁) = 20 × ln 3 = 21.97 kJ
Into vacuum: P<sub>ext</sub> = 0, so W = 0
Isobaric gives most, but its end state (2 bar, T tripled) differs from the isothermal end state (0.667 bar); the maximum-work rule compares paths between the same end states
The three answers show W is a path function
answer: Convention and data. W is work done by the gas, W = ∫P dV for a slow (quasi-static) process and ∫P<sub>ext</sub> dV for a sudden one. P₁ = 2 bar = 200 kPa, V₁ = 0.1 m³, V₂ = 0.3 m³. With P in kPa and V in m³, W comes out in kJ.

answer.text: (a) Isobaric at 200 kPa.
answer.pre:
W = P (V₂ − V₁) = 200 × (0.3 − 0.1) = 40.0 kJ
end state: 2 bar, 0.3 m³; for an ideal gas T₂ = 3T₁

answer.text: (b) Reversible isothermal, ideal gas: PV = P₁V₁ = 20 kJ all along the path.
answer.pre:
W = ∫P dV = P₁V₁ ln(V₂/V₁) = 20 × ln 3 = 20 × 1.0986 = 21.97 kJ
end state: P₂ = P₁V₁/V₂ = 200 × 0.1/0.3 = 66.7 kPa = 0.667 bar, T₂ = T₁

answer: (c) Expansion into a vacuum (free expansion). The gas pushes against nothing: P<sub>ext</sub> = 0, so W = ∫P<sub>ext</sub> dV = 0 although the volume triples. ∫P dV cannot be used, because the gas pressure is not defined during the sudden rush and nothing resists it.

answer.text: Compare.

answer: Heat in each case. Isothermal: ΔU = 0, so Q = W = 21.97 kJ enters as heat. Free expansion: Q = 0, W = 0, ΔU = 0. Isobaric: the temperature triples, so heat larger than the 40 kJ of work must be supplied (Q = ΔU + W, with ΔU > 0).

Resolve the question. The isobaric path gives the most work, 40 kJ, because heat is added to keep the pressure at 2 bar and the gas ends three times hotter. The rule "reversible gives the most work" compares paths between the same two end states. Paths (b) and (c) do share an end state (0.667 bar, T₁): there the reversible path gives 21.97 kJ and the irreversible free expansion gives 0, as the rule says. Path (a) ends somewhere else, so the rule does not apply to it. All three start at the same state and reach the same volume, yet give 40, 21.97 and 0 kJ: work is a path function.

bank.q: Derive the steady-flow energy equation for an open system and explain why enthalpy appears in it while the closed-system balance uses internal energy. Show that the flow-work term Pv is the reason for the shift.
outline: Take a control volume, apply conservation of mass and of energy over a time interval
Work terms: shaft work W<sub>s</sub> plus work done by the fluid on the fluid ahead (flow work Pv)
E<sub>in</sub> − E<sub>out</sub> = ΔU + ΔKE + ΔPE per unit mass plus flow work
Combine u + Pv = h
Q − W<sub>s</sub> = ṁ[Δh + Δ(c²/2) + gΔz]
For a closed system the boundary moves with the mass so Pv terms cancel
Check limiting cases: no flow gives ΔU = Q − W; Q = W<sub>s</sub> = 0 in a nozzle gives h<sub>1</sub> + c<sub>1</sub>²/2 = h<sub>2</sub> + c<sub>2</sub>²/2
answer: Set up the control volume. A fixed region with one inlet (section 1) and one outlet (section 2), a shaft, and heat crossing the walls. Q is heat added, W<sub>s</sub> shaft work done by the fluid. Consider a short time dt in which mass dm₁ enters and dm₂ leaves.
Mass balance. Mass inside changes by dm₁ − dm₂. At steady flow nothing inside changes, so dm₁ = dm₂ = ṁ dt.

answer.text: Count the work at the openings. To push the element dm₁ (volume v₁dm₁) into the control volume, the fluid behind it pushes with force P₁A₁ through the distance v₁dm₁/A₁, doing work P₁v₁dm₁ on the system. At the outlet the system does P₂v₂dm₂ on the fluid ahead. This is flow work; it exists only because mass crosses the boundary.
answer.pre: flow work in  = P₁v₁ dm₁      flow work out = P₂v₂ dm₂

answer.text: Energy balance over dt. Energy stored per kilogram of stream is e = u + c²/2 + gz.
answer.pre: dE<sub>cv</sub> = δQ − δW<sub>s</sub> + (u₁ + c₁²/2 + gz₁ + P₁v₁) dm₁ − (u₂ + c₂²/2 + gz₂ + P₂v₂) dm₂

answer.text: Group u + Pv into h, then apply steady flow (dE<sub>cv</sub> = 0, dm₁ = dm₂ = ṁ dt) and divide by dt:
answer.pre:
h = u + Pv
Q − W<sub>s</sub> = ṁ[(h₂ − h₁) + (c₂² − c₁²)/2 + g(z₂ − z₁)]

answer: Why the closed system uses U. In a closed system no mass crosses the boundary, so there are no flow-work terms; any moving boundary work is included in W. The Pv terms appear only with mass flow, and because they always ride with u in each stream, it is natural to combine them into one property h. That is the only reason enthalpy replaces internal energy.

answer.text: Check limiting cases and a number.

head: Case
Terms set to zero
Result
rows: ṁ, flow work; moving-boundary work in W

bank.q: A student argues: since Q and W depend on the path, the first law ΔU = Q − W means internal energy must also depend on the path. Examine this argument and explain what makes ΔU path-independent. Include a cyclic process in your answer.
outline: Identify the error: Q and W change together so their difference is path-independent
State exact-differential test for dU versus δQ and δW
Illustrate with two paths between the same states: different Q, different W, same ΔU
Cycle: ∮dU = 0 while ∮δQ = ∮δW ≠ 0
Joule's experiment as experimental evidence
Consequence: property tables and equations of state are possible
Strength/limitation: first law alone does not say which direction a process can go — that needs the second law
answer: Find the error. The argument assumes that because Q and W each depend on the path, their difference must too. It does not follow: Q and W can change together in such a way that Q − W stays the same. Experiment (Joule) shows that they do.

answer.text: Use the exactness test. With T and V as variables for one mole of ideal gas, dU = C<sub>v</sub> dT passes the test, while δW = (RT/V) dV fails it (∂(RT/V)/∂T = R/V ≠ 0), and so does δQ = C<sub>v</sub> dT + (RT/V) dV. The sum of two inexact differentials can be exact:
answer.pre: dU = δQ − δW = [C<sub>v</sub> dT + (RT/V) dV] − (RT/V) dV = C<sub>v</sub> dT   (exact)

answer.text: Show it with two paths (ideal gas from A at 3 kPa, 1 L to B at 1 kPa, 3 L; PV is 3 J at both ends, so T and U are the same at A and B).

answer: Make a cycle. Go A → B along path A and return along path B reversed. ∮δW = 3.50 − 4.00 = −0.50 J and ∮δQ = −0.50 J, both non-zero; ∮dU = 0. A cycle returns every property to its starting value, so a quantity with a non-zero cyclic integral cannot be a property, while ∮dU = 0 for every cycle is what makes U one.

Experimental evidence. Joule raised the temperature of insulated water by the same amount with different combinations of falling mass and height, and the same rise could be produced by heating. The end state, and so ΔU, fixed the energy needed, whatever mix of work and heat supplied it. The cyclic statement ∮δQ = ∮δW is the general form of this observation, and ΔU = Q − W follows from it.

Consequences. Because U is a property, it can be tabulated (steam tables, property charts) and calculated along any convenient path, real or hypothetical, between the same end states; that is how ΔU of a sudden irreversible process is found.

Limitation of the first law. It fixes the energy balance but not the direction: it allows heat to flow from cold to hot or a free expansion to reverse itself, as long as energy is conserved. Deciding which processes can actually happen needs the second law and entropy.

bank.q: Compare a throttling valve, a nozzle and a compressor as steady-flow devices. For each, write the reduced energy equation, state the assumptions and explain where the energy goes.
outline: All three: steady flow, single inlet and outlet, neglect ΔPE
Throttling: Q = 0, W = 0, ΔKE ≈ 0 → h<sub>1</sub> = h<sub>2</sub>, isenthalpic; pressure drops through friction, irreversible
Nozzle: Q = 0, W = 0 → enthalpy converts into kinetic energy, pressure and temperature fall
Compressor: ΔKE small, Q small → W<sub>s</sub> ≈ Δh, work input raises pressure and enthalpy
Identify which terms may be dropped and why; mention typical assumptions of negligible heat loss
Compare reversibility: nozzle and diffuser designed near-isentropic, throttling fully irreversible

answer.text: Common assumptions. Steady flow, one inlet and one outlet, height change negligible. Per kilogram, with w<sub>s</sub> work done by the fluid:
answer.pre: h₁ + c₁²/2 + q = h₂ + c₂²/2 + w<sub>s</sub>

answer.text: Throttling valve. No shaft (w<sub>s</sub> = 0); the valve is small and the flow fast, so q ≈ 0; inlet and outlet pipes are sized so that c₁ ≈ c₂.

answer: Where the energy goes in the valve: nowhere. The pressure drop is used up in friction and eddies, which turn ordered flow energy into internal energy of the same fluid. An ideal gas keeps its temperature (air throttled from 5 bar, 300 K to 1 bar stays at 300 K); a real gas usually cools a little (the Joule–Thomson effect, the basis of refrigeration expansion valves). The process is completely irreversible: the pressure is lost and nothing is gained for it.

answer.text: Nozzle. No shaft, nearly adiabatic, but the speed changes a lot:
answer.pre:
h₁ + c₁²/2 = h₂ + c₂²/2
example: h₁ = 300, h₂ = 280 kJ/kg, c₁ = 50 m/s → c₂ = 206.2 m/s

answer: Where the energy goes in the nozzle: enthalpy turns into kinetic energy. The fluid speeds up, and its enthalpy, temperature and pressure fall. A well-designed nozzle is close to isentropic (reversible and adiabatic), and a diffuser does the reverse.

answer.text: Compressor. Large pipes, so c₁ ≈ c₂; heat loss usually small:
answer.pre:
w<sub>in</sub> = −w<sub>s</sub> = h₂ − h₁ − q
example: air 1 → 5 bar, 300 K, η<sub>c</sub> = 0.80: w<sub>in</sub> = 220.0 kJ/kg, T₂ = 518.9 K

answer: Where the energy goes in the compressor: shaft work turns into enthalpy (higher pressure and temperature). Some extra work is lost in friction, which is why the real machine needs 220.0 kJ/kg against 176.0 for the isentropic ideal.

answer.text: Summary.

answer: When terms may be dropped. Estimate each one: a speed change of 100 m/s is 5 kJ/kg; a height change of 10 m is 0.1 kJ/kg; casing heat loss is usually a few per cent of the work. Drop a term only when it is a small fraction of the main enthalpy change.

bank.q: Choose a control volume for a steam turbine in a power plant and carry out a full energy accounting for it. Discuss which terms you may neglect, how you would estimate the heat loss, and what the first law alone cannot tell you about the turbine's performance.
outline: Draw the control volume around the turbine casing with inlet, outlet and shaft
Write Q − W<sub>s</sub> = m[Δh + ΔKE + ΔPE]
Neglect ΔPE; check whether ΔKE is significant against Δh
Shaft work from the enthalpy drop; sign convention for work out
Estimate casing heat loss from insulation and surface temperature, show it is small but not zero
First law gives quantity of work only, not the best possible work — need the second law and isentropic efficiency
Practical points: steam quality at exit, condensate, unit consistency
answer: Draw the control volume around the turbine casing, cutting the steam inlet pipe (1), the exhaust (2) and the shaft. Mark Q (heat into the steam, here a loss) and W<sub>s</sub> (shaft power out, positive). Use the worked example data: ṁ = 2.0 kg/s, h₁ = 3200 kJ/kg, c₁ = 60 m/s, h₂ = 2600 kJ/kg, c₂ = 120 m/s.

answer.text: Write the full balance:
answer.pre: Q − W<sub>s</sub> = ṁ[(h₂ − h₁) + (c₂² − c₁²)/2 + g(z₂ − z₁)]

answer.text: Size each term per kilogram before dropping anything (assume the exhaust is 3 m below the inlet).

answer: Decide what to neglect. Δpe is negligible. Δke is under 1 % here, so it may be dropped for a quick estimate, but it is kept below because it is easy; with a high exhaust velocity (large last-stage blades, 200 to 300 m/s) it would not be negligible.

answer.text: Estimate the heat loss. Q = h<sub>o</sub>A(T<sub>surface</sub> − T<sub>air</sub>), with assumed values: insulated casing area A = 25 m², outer surface 70 °C, air 30 °C, combined convection-plus-radiation coefficient h<sub>o</sub> ≈ 12 W/(m²·K).
answer.pre:
Q ≈ 12 × 25 × (70 − 30) = 12 000 W = 12 kW lost   (Q = −12 kW)
worked example used Q = −50 kW, a casing with poorer insulation

answer.text: Shaft power with both heat-loss values.

answer: Sign check. W<sub>s</sub> is positive, so work leaves the steam, as it must for a turbine; heat loss reduces the work available from the same enthalpy drop.

What the first law cannot say. It gives the quantity of work for the measured inlet and exit states, not the best possible work. Suppose the isentropic exit enthalpy at the same exhaust pressure, read from a Mollier chart, is 2450 kJ/kg. Then the ideal drop is 750 kJ/kg and the isentropic efficiency is η<sub>t</sub> = 600/750 = 0.80: 20 % of the available drop is lost to friction and leakage. Finding h₂s and judging that loss needs entropy and the second law.

Practical points. At the exhaust of a condensing turbine the steam is usually wet: its quality must be checked because droplets erode the last blades. Keep units consistent (kJ/kg × kg/s = kW; c²/2 in J/kg ÷ 1000). Measure h from pressure and temperature only where the steam is superheated; in the wet region temperature alone does not fix the state.

bank.q: An insulated rigid tank is divided into two parts by a partition; one side holds a compressed gas and the other is evacuated. The partition is removed and the gas fills the tank. Analyse the process using the first law, state the assumptions, and comment on whether the gas temperature changes for an ideal gas.
outline: Closed system, rigid: W = 0; insulated: Q = 0 → ΔU = 0
Free expansion is highly irreversible, not a reversible adiabatic path
For an ideal gas U depends on T only, so T is unchanged and P falls as V increases
For a real gas, U depends on V too, so T changes (Joule coefficient)
Contrast with reversible adiabatic expansion where T falls
Note that the energy balance gives the answer without knowing the intermediate states
answer: System and assumptions. The whole tank (both halves) is the system: closed, since no mass crosses its outer wall. Rigid, so no boundary work; no shaft or electrical work: W = 0. Insulated: Q = 0. The tank does not move: ΔKE = ΔPE = 0. Take numbers: air (ideal gas, R = 0.287 kJ/(kg·K), c<sub>v</sub> = 0.718 kJ/(kg·K)) at 400 kPa and 300 K fills one half of 0.5 m³; the other half of 0.5 m³ is empty.

answer.text: First law.

answer: Nature of the process. When the partition breaks, the gas rushes into the vacuum with large pressure and velocity differences; it passes through no equilibrium states, so it is highly irreversible and cannot be drawn as a line on a P–V diagram. The first law still applies, because it needs only the end states. Work is zero because nothing outside the gas is pushed.

answer.text: Ideal gas. U depends on T only, so ΔU = 0 gives ΔT = 0.
Contrast with a reversible adiabatic expansion to the same volume (a piston pushed out slowly, PV<sup>1.4</sup> constant):

answer: Compare. Both processes are adiabatic and end at 1.0 m³, but the reversible one does 121.2 kJ of work and cools the gas by 72.6 K, while the free expansion does no work and leaves the temperature unchanged. Q = 0 alone does not fix the final state; the work does.

Real gas. In a real gas U depends slightly on volume too, because the molecules attract each other. When the gas spreads out, work is done against these attractions at the expense of molecular kinetic energy, so most real gases cool slightly in a free expansion (the Joule coefficient (∂T/∂V)<sub>U</sub> is negative). Joule could not measure this with air at low pressure, which is why the result is stated exactly only for an ideal gas.
Conclusion. Q = 0, W = 0, ΔU = 0; for an ideal gas the temperature stays at 300 K and the pressure halves to 200 kPa. The energy balance gives this without knowing any intermediate state.

glossary.def: No heat crosses the boundary, Q = 0.
The surface, real or imaginary, that separates the system from its surroundings and across which heat, work and mass are counted.
A system of fixed mass in which no mass crosses the boundary.
A fixed region in space, with mass able to flow in and out, used for open-system analysis.
A wall that allows heat to pass so that two bodies can reach thermal equilibrium.
H = U + PV, a state function convenient for constant-pressure and flow processes.
A property proportional to the quantity of matter, such as mass, volume or total internal energy.
The Pv work a flowing fluid does on the fluid ahead of it and receives from the fluid behind it.
Energy transferred across a boundary because of a temperature difference.
The heat needed to raise the temperature of a unit amount by one kelvin, at constant volume or constant pressure.
A property independent of size, such as temperature, pressure or density.
The total kinetic and potential energy of the molecules of the system, a state function whose changes are measurable.
A real process with friction, finite gradients or unrestrained expansion that cannot be undone without external work.
A system that exchanges neither mass nor energy with the surroundings.
The SI unit of thermodynamic temperature; since 2019 it is fixed by the Boltzmann constant, and the triple point of water is 273.16 K to within a fraction of a millikelvin.
An extensive property divided by the number of moles, in units per mole.
A duct shaped so that the fluid speeds up while its enthalpy and pressure fall: converging for subsonic flow, converging–diverging to pass sonic speed.
A system in which mass crosses the boundary, also called a control volume.
A quantity whose value between two states depends on the route, such as heat and work.
An idealised process through continuous equilibrium states that can be reversed exactly by an infinitesimal change in the surroundings.
An extensive property divided by mass, in units per kilogram.
A property fixed by the state of the system, so its change depends only on the end states.
A flow in which properties at any point do not change with time, so mass and energy within the control volume stay constant.
If two bodies are each in thermal equilibrium with a third, they are in thermal equilibrium with each other, which justifies temperature as a property.
A pressure drop through a valve or porous plug with no work and negligible heat, so h<sub>1</sub> = h<sub>2</sub>.
Flow speed divided by the local speed of sound, Ma = c/a with a = √(γRT) for an ideal gas.
Flow in which the throat has reached sonic speed, so lowering the back pressure no longer raises the mass flow.
For a compressor, isentropic work over actual work; for a turbine, actual work over isentropic work.
